page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.sn1ne.xlarge is a compute-optimized virtual machine instance powered by the KVM hypervisor. It features 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 cores running at 2.5 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The system is equipped with 8.0 GB of system memory, providing a resource density of 2.0 GB per core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 2 Gbps.

Benchmark evaluations place the performance of the ecs.sn1ne.xlarge in the lower tiers. In CPU-intensive tasks, stress-ng single-core and multi-core tests rank the instance in the bottom 25%, a trend mirrored by its PassMark CPU score. Memory subsystem performance is also constrained, with large-block read-only memory bandwidth registering in the bottom 10% and write bandwidth in the bottom 25%. Real-world application simulations, such as Redis SET operations and static web serving throughput, similarly fall into the bottom 10% of tested systems.

Given its dedicated CPU allocation but older Intel Xeon architecture, this instance offers an entry-level compute profile. It is best suited for lightweight utility workloads, basic development environments, or low-traffic web serving where dedicated CPU resources are required but high memory capacity or modern instruction set performance is not critical.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.sn1ne.xlarge is a compute-optimized virtual machine instance featuring 4 dedicated vCPUs and 8.0 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 processor running at 2.5 GHz on the x86_64 architecture, this KVM-based instance provides a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. It does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and it operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 2 Gbps. Performance benchmarks, including stress-ng and Geekbench, consistently place this instance in the lower performance tiers, with memory bandwidth and database operations scoring in the bottom 10% to 25%. Consequently, the ecs.sn1ne.xlarge is best utilized for lightweight, non-critical workloads, basic development environments, and low-traffic utility services that require dedicated CPU allocation without demanding high memory density or modern processor architectures.
